lead: A circuit with both an inductor and a capacitor has two energy stores, so after a switch it can do more than decay: it can overshoot and ring. The governing equation is second order, and its two roots decide the shape. Overdamped means two real roots and a slow creep; critically damped means one repeated root and the fastest rise without overshoot; underdamped means complex roots and a damped sine. This explains relay chatter, filter settling, motor drive overshoot and the ring you see on a lab oscilloscope.
prereq: You need: initial and final conditions for the t = 0 state and first-order step response for forced plus natural thinking.

sections.h3: The characteristic equation and the three shapes

blocks.text: A series RLC circuit with a DC step source has two energy stores, L and C. Write v<sub>C</sub>(t) for the capacitor voltage and V<sub>s</sub> for the step height. After the switch the circuit satisfies LC v<sub>C</sub>'' + RC v<sub>C</sub>' + v<sub>C</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>. Divide by LC. The forced part is V<sub>s</sub>; the natural part is set by s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = 0. Define α and ω₀ so the same equation reads s² + 2αs + ω₀² = 0.

blocks.where: s₁ and s₂ are the natural frequencies in s⁻¹; α is the damping coefficient in s⁻¹; ω₀ is the undamped natural frequency in rad/s.

items: α > ω₀: two different real negative roots. The circuit is overdamped; v<sub>C</sub> creeps to V<sub>s</sub> with two decaying exponentials.
α = ω₀: one repeated real root −α. The circuit is critically damped; v<sub>C</sub> rises as fast as possible without overshoot.
α < ω₀: complex roots −α ± jω_d with ω<sub>d</sub> = √(ω₀² − α²). The circuit is underdamped; v<sub>C</sub> overshoots and rings at ω<sub>d</sub>.

blocks.text: Compare α with ω₀, or, if you prefer, α² with ω₀²; the two tests are the same because both numbers are positive. α = 12 s⁻¹ with ω₀ = 10 rad/s is overdamped: 12 > 10, and also 144 > 100. Equality is one point, not a range. Some syllabi write over-damped, critically damped and under-damped.
The same test is often written with the damping ratio ζ = α/ω₀, a pure number, which Figure 5.4.1 gives for each curve: ζ < 1 underdamped, ζ = 1 critical, ζ > 1 overdamped.

The same quadratic appears in series and parallel RLC, but α is read differently. For a series RLC with resistance R, inductance L and capacitance C, α = R/(2L). For a parallel RLC, α = 1/(2RC). In both, ω₀ = 1/√(LC). Use the series value only for series circuits and the parallel value only for parallel circuits.
α<sub>series</sub> and α<sub>parallel</sub> are damping coefficients in s⁻¹; R is resistance in ohms; L is inductance in henries; C is capacitance in farads; ω₀ is in rad/s.

Write V<sub>f</sub> for the final capacitor voltage; for the series voltage step V<sub>f</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>. With a DC step from zero initial energy, the full capacitor voltage takes one of three forms. Overdamped: v<sub>C</sub>(t) = V<sub>f</sub> + A₁e<sup>s₁t</sup> + A₂e<sup>s₂t</sup>. Critically damped: v<sub>C</sub>(t) = V<sub>f</sub> + (A₁ + A₂t)e<sup>−αt</sup>. Underdamped: v<sub>C</sub>(t) = V<sub>f</sub> + e<sup>−αt</sup>(A₁cos ω<sub>d</sub> t + A₂sin ω<sub>d</sub> t). The constants A₁ and A₂ are fixed by v<sub>C</sub>(0) and v<sub>C</sub>'(0).

The initial conditions come from the two storage elements. Capacitor voltage cannot jump: v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻). Inductor current cannot jump: i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻). For a series circuit the current through C is the same as the inductor current, so v<sub>C</sub>'(0⁺) = i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺)/C. For a parallel circuit, find the capacitor current at 0⁺ by KCL, then use v<sub>C</sub>'(0⁺) = i<sub>C</sub>(0⁺)/C.

The shape has a physical meaning. In the underdamped case energy swaps between L and C, so v<sub>C</sub> overshoots V<sub>f</sub> and rings; R removes energy each cycle, so the ring decays as e<sup>−αt</sup>. In the critically damped case the circuit returns to rest as fast as it can without a second overshoot. In the overdamped case one exponential dies quickly and the other lingers, so the rise is slow. A larger R in a series circuit increases α and pushes the same circuit from underdamped to critical to overdamped.

Use the response to choose R. A contactor coil or a filter that must not ring is made overdamped or critical. A radio front end may want a sharp underdamped response. The same three words describe mechanical suspension and control loops.

figure.caption: The worked example: the capacitor voltage of the same series circuit (L = 1 H, C = 0.01 F, 10 V step) for three resistances. With 4 Ω it overshoots to 15.27 V and rings; with 20 Ω it rises fastest without overshoot; with 40 Ω it creeps up slowly.

spec.aria: Plot of capacitor voltage against time from 0 to 2 seconds for R equal to 4, 20 and 40 ohms: an underdamped curve peaking at 15.27 volts at 0.321 seconds, a critically damped curve and a slow overdamped curve, all settling to 10 volts.

examples.question: A series RLC circuit has L = 1 H, C = 0.01 F and a 10 V DC step source. The capacitor is initially uncharged and the inductor current is zero. Find ω₀ and α for R = 4 Ω, R = 20 Ω and R = 40 Ω. Name the damping case in each. For R = 4 Ω, also find the damped frequency ω<sub>d</sub>.
steps: For a series circuit use α = R/(2L) = R/(2 × 1) = R/2 s⁻¹.
R = 4 Ω: α = 2 s⁻¹. α² = 4 and ω₀² = 100, so α < ω₀. Underdamped.
R = 20 Ω: α = 10 s⁻¹. α² = 100 = ω₀². Critically damped.
R = 40 Ω: α = 20 s⁻¹. α² = 400 > 100. Overdamped.
For R = 4 Ω, ω<sub>d</sub> = √(ω₀² − α²) = √(100 − 4) = √96 = 9.80 rad/s.
examples.answer: ω₀ = 10 rad/s; for R = 4, 20 and 40 Ω, α = 2, 10 and 20 s⁻¹ (ζ = 0.2, 1 and 2), so the cases are underdamped, critically damped and overdamped; for R = 4 Ω, ω<sub>d</sub> = 9.80 rad/s.
examples.check:
import math
L = 1.0
C = 0.01
w0 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(L * C)
print(w0)
Rs = [4.0, 20.0, 40.0]
alphas = [R / (2.0 * L) for R in Rs]
for a in alphas:
    print(a)
zetas = [a / w0 for a in alphas]
for z in zetas:
    print(z)
wd = math.sqrt(w0 * w0 - alphas[0] * alphas[0])
print(round(wd, 3))

examples.question: For the R = 4 Ω case of the first example (L = 1 H, C = 0.01 F, 10 V step, nothing stored), find v<sub>C</sub>(t), the time of the first peak and the peak voltage.
steps: Underdamped with α = 2 s⁻¹ and ω<sub>d</sub> = 9.80 rad/s, so v<sub>C</sub>(t) = 10 + e<sup>−2t</sup>(A₁ cos 9.80t + A₂ sin 9.80t).
i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = 0 and i = C dv<sub>C</sub>/dt, so dv<sub>C</sub>/dt(0⁺) = 0. Differentiating at t = 0: −αA₁ + ω<sub>d</sub> A₂ = 0, so A₂ = αA₁/ω<sub>d</sub> = (2 × −10)/9.80 = −2.04.
v<sub>C</sub>(t) = 10 − e<sup>−2t</sup>(10 cos 9.80t + 2.04 sin 9.80t) V. Check: v<sub>C</sub>(0) = 10 − 10 = 0 ✓ and v<sub>C</sub>(∞) = 10 V ✓.
The first peak comes at ω<sub>d</sub> t = π: t = π/9.80 = 0.321 s. There cos = −1 and sin = 0, so v<sub>C</sub> = 10 + 10 e<sup>−0.641</sup> = 10 + 5.27 = 15.27 V.
examples.answer: v<sub>C</sub>(t) = 10 − e<sup>−2t</sup>(10 cos 9.80t + 2.04 sin 9.80t) V; the first peak is 15.27 V at t = 0.321 s, an overshoot of 52.7 %.
examples.check:
import math
wd=math.sqrt(96); A2=2*-10/wd; tp=math.pi/wd
print(wd,A2,tp,10+10*math.exp(-2*tp))

traps: Using α = 1/(2RC) in a series RLC circuit; the series value is R/(2L).
Squaring only one side. Compare α with ω₀ (the easy test), or α² with ω₀², but never α² with ω₀. α = 12 s⁻¹ with ω₀ = 10 rad/s is overdamped: 12 > 10 and 144 > 100.
Letting v<sub>C</sub> or i<sub>L</sub> jump at the switch; both are continuous, and their 0⁻ values set the constants.
Writing ω<sub>d</sub> = √(α² − ω₀²); for underdamped it is √(ω₀² − α²), a real positive number.

quiz.q: Write the characteristic equation of a series RLC circuit in terms of α and ω₀.
quiz.a: s² + 2αs + ω₀² = 0, with α = R/(2L) and ω₀ = 1/√(LC).

quiz.q: Why is the critically damped response the fastest one that does not overshoot?
quiz.a: With less damping (underdamped) the response rises faster but overshoots. With more damping (overdamped) the slow root −α + √(α² − ω₀²) moves towards zero, so the response creeps. Critical damping, the repeated root −α, is the boundary: the quickest rise that still has no overshoot.

quiz.q: A series RLC has L = 2 H, C = 0.02 F and R = 20 Ω. Find ω₀, α and the damping case.
quiz.a: ω₀ = 1/√(2 × 0.02) = 1/0.2 = 5 rad/s. α = R/(2L) = 20/4 = 5 s⁻¹. α = ω₀, so the circuit is critically damped.

quiz.q: A parallel RLC has R = 50 Ω, L = 0.2 H and C = 0.002 F. Find α, ω₀ and the case. What happens to α if R is doubled?
quiz.a: ω₀ = 1/√(0.2 × 0.002) = 1/√0.0004 = 50 rad/s. α = 1/(2RC) = 1/(2 × 50 × 0.002) = 5 s⁻¹. α < ω₀, so underdamped. With R = 100 Ω, α = 2.5 s⁻¹: still underdamped and less damped.

quiz.q: For the R = 4 Ω example, write v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) and dv<sub>C</sub>/dt at 0⁺.
quiz.a: v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = 0 V because capacitor voltage cannot jump. i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = 0 A, and in series dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = i<sub>L</sub>/C, so dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = 0 V/s at 0⁺.

quiz.q: Why does a larger series R move the circuit toward overdamped?
quiz.a: For a series circuit α = R/(2L), so larger R gives larger α. The real roots appear when α > ω₀, which is the overdamped condition.

quiz.q: An underdamped response has ω₀ = 100 rad/s and α = 6 s⁻¹. Find ω<sub>d</sub> and the time constant of the decay envelope.
quiz.a: ω<sub>d</sub> = √(ω₀² − α²) = √(10000 − 36) = √9964 ≈ 99.82 rad/s. The envelope is e<sup>−6t</sup>, so its time constant is 1/6 ≈ 0.1667 s.

beyond: Not for the exam. In control and filter design the same second-order model is written with ζ and ω<sub>n</sub>; percent overshoot and settling time follow from those two numbers. Power-electronic snubbers and EMI filters are chosen by these damping cases. MEMS accelerometers and loudspeaker crossovers also show underdamped ring. Search next for second-order step response damping ratio, RLC settling time, and series RLC step response derivation.
